Every raindrop starts as water on the ground. To fall from the sky, it first has to get up there, and it makes the trip as a gas.
Liquid becomes vapour
Evaporation is the change from liquid water into water vapour, a gas. It happens when heat breaks the bonds that hold water molecules together.
The vapour mixes into the air and cannot be seen. The water has not gone anywhere: it is now part of the air around us.
Where the vapour comes from
About 90 percent of the moisture in the air came from water evaporating from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers.
Oceans cover more than 70 percent of Earth's surface, which is why so much of that moisture comes from them.
Heat turns water into vapour, the vapour is carried up into a cloud, and the cloud can rain on the land.
The next lesson follows this vapour as it rises, cools and turns back into liquid by condensation. That is how a cloud is made. You can read ahead in the glossary or go to lesson 2.
Rain starts as water on the ground.
Heat turns it into water vapour, a gas you cannot see.
Most of that vapour comes from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers.
The vapour from the last lesson does not stay a gas for ever. High in the sky it turns back into liquid water, and that is what a cloud is made of.
Rising air cools
Clouds form because air containing water vapour rises and cools. As the air rises it is under less pressure, so it spreads out and gets cooler.
Cooling to the dew point
Clouds form when the air cools below the dew point, and water vapour condenses to liquid water.
Condensation is the change from water vapour back into liquid water. It is the opposite of evaporation.
Try it at home
On a humid day, a glass of iced water collects drops on its outside. The air touching the cold glass cools, and its vapour condenses.
Every droplet needs a seed
Vapour condenses more easily when it has a particle to settle on. Tiny bits of dust, salt, smoke and pollen do this job, and they are called condensation nuclei.
Follow one parcel of air
Warm, damp air near the sea starts to rise.
Higher up there is less pressure, so the air spreads out and cools.
It cools below its dew point.
Its vapour condenses on specks of dust and salt.
Together, the tiny droplets make a cloud.
A rising parcel of air spreads out and cools. Past its dew point, the vapour condenses into droplets.
Damp air rises, spreads out and cools.
Once it cools below the dew point, its vapour condenses.
Each droplet forms on a speck of dust, salt, smoke or pollen, and together they make a cloud.
Rain is one kind of precipitation: water released from clouds as rain, freezing rain, sleet, snow or hail.
The droplets in a cloud are far too small to fall as rain. To reach the ground, they have to grow.
Droplets merge
Droplets bump into each other and join together, which is called coalescence. Millions of cloud droplets are needed to make a single raindrop.
A drop leaves the cloud once it falls faster than the updraft, the rising air inside the cloud.
The ice route
When a cloud holds ice crystals, the crystals can grow quickly by taking water from the cloud. This is called the Bergeron process.
The crystals may fall as snow, or melt on the way down and fall as rain.
The shape of a raindrop
Raindrops are not shaped like teardrops. Small drops, with a radius under 1 millimetre, are round like a ball.
At about 2 to 3 millimetres across, a falling drop is flat underneath, like a hamburger bun.
At about 4 to 5 millimetres, the dip in its bottom grows into a shape like a parachute.
Bigger still, the drop breaks up into smaller drops.
As a falling drop grows, air pushes its bottom flat, then hollows it out, until it splits.
Cloud droplets are too small to fall, so they have to grow.
They merge, and millions of them make one raindrop.
In icy clouds, crystals grow fast and fall as snow, or melt into rain.
Small raindrops are round, and big ones flatten and break apart.
